name: earth-day-night
title: The Earth right now: a textured globe with day, night and city lights
summary: A turning 3D globe textured with a 768 x 384 map made from the catalog's own Natural Earth data, lit by a sun placed where it really is at the current clock (declination and equation of time from dayOfYear(), the subsolar longitude from UTC), so the day/night terminator is real; 16 cities are dots (one merged mesh) that glow on the night side, six carry labels projected from 3D to the screen, and a drag spins and tilts it.
prompt: Show the Earth as a 3D globe that turns, with the continents, the real day and night for right now, and a few cities as dots; let me drag to spin it.
hand_built: Scene3D has no texture or sun; a textured sphere, a light from the computed sun direction, city dots lit from the night side and labels projected to the screen need the 3D ops by hand.
teaches: Texture a sphere: meshPrimitive3D sphere with "uv": "uv", texture3D on a bitmap resource, white paint, drawMesh3D smooth (the same approach as the textured globes of hoford.github.io/RemoteCompose-Examples, render/textured-sphere and vis-set-10)

Make the texture fit the primitive's UV, not the other way round: the sphere's u is 1 - φ/2π with φ the angle from +X toward +Z, so an equirectangular map whose left edge is Greenwich and which runs east puts longitude λ at (cos λ, ·, -sin λ) with no extra rotation, and world space is Earth-fixed

Place the sun from the clock: declination -23.44° · cos(2π(N + 10)/365), equation of time 9.87 sin 2B - 7.53 cos B - 1.5 sin B, subsolar longitude (720 - UTC minutes - EoT)/4 degrees; the directional light travels along minus that vector

Get a real terminator: with material3D specular above 0 the lighting is one-sided (a face turned away from the light gets ambient only), while specular 0 lights both sides (|N·L|) and the night disappears
Turn the camera, not the globe (lights are in world space): the eye orbits at D·(cos t sin s, sin t, cos t cos s), s from an autorotation, the drag and the sun's longitude

Draw fixed points as one mesh: the 16 city dots are small octahedra merged into a single defineMesh3D (2.3 KB), because each drawMesh3D composites the whole window buffer (a loop of 16 sphere draws cost the TypeScript player about 68 ms a frame at 1080 x 1920, the merged mesh a few); lit from the anti-sun direction, they glow on the night side and are dim by day

Label 3D points in 2D: project each city with the camera basis (right (cos s, 0, -sin s), up (-sin t sin s, cos t, -sin t cos s)) and F = (H/2)/tan(fov/2), and push the label off screen with step() when it is behind the limb
Frame the globe in the free part of the window: the distance D = 1/sin(atan(r/F)) for a target radius r in px, and a 2D translate before the 3D moves the window-sized buffer to the free region

Draw line art on a sphere in mono with a mostly transparent texture (texels with alpha 0 are skipped and write no depth), then the hidden-line wireframe: its own depth prepass hides the back, and objects drawn after it (dots, the terminator ring) stay visible as long as no negative depthBias3D was active during the wireframe
Keep labels readable over a globe and a page of either theme: draw every label first as a 3-px stroke in a dark halo colour (the background in mono), then the fill on top
pitfalls: 3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming): this plays in the C++ and TypeScript players only

The texture is most of the size: 21.7 KB of the document is the 768 x 384 colour map (10-colour palette PNG); a 1024 x 512 map with 1:50m coastlines costs 32 KB. Nearest-texel sampling shows the texels at the coast when the globe is large
Ambient light is a fixed 0.2, so the night side stays dimly visible and cannot be made darker
In the TypeScript web player bitmaps decode asynchronously: the globe can draw untextured for its first frame
The sun uses minute resolution (timeInMin()) and offsetToUtc(); with a wrong device time zone the terminator is wrong by the same amount
The labels are 2D text projected by hand: they are not hidden by the city's own dot or clipped at the limb, only switched off a little before it
The texture is stylised (land, ice, shelf, a 30° graticule from Natural Earth), not a satellite image

A wireframe drawMesh3D fills the z-buffer with its front faces first; with a negative depthBias3D active it writes them biased toward the eye, so later parts close to the surface (city dots, a ring 0.004 above it) disappear. Draw the wireframe without a bias (its prepass already hides the back lines) when anything sits on the surface afterwards

The globe itself is the same in light and dark (the texture is a bitmap and the night side is physical); the page, text and stars follow the theme. The halo is a radial gradient of literal colours (gradients take no themed colours) chosen to read on both
java_difference: 3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming): the Java JSON parser does not know camera3D, lights3D, matrix3D, meshPrimitive3D or drawMesh3D; plays in the C++ and TypeScript players

snippets.note: the sun light, specular for a one-sided terminator, texture3D and the draw; mono: land mask over a hidden-line graticule
sun declination, equation of time and subsolar longitude from the clock
all 16 city dots as one defineMesh3D of small octahedra

assets: Texture generated for this example from assets/maps/maps.json (Natural Earth 1:50m land and 1:110m lakes, public domain): equirectangular 768 x 384, Greenwich at the left edge, quantised to 10 colours. The mono texture is the 1:110m coastline drawn as lines into a 512 x 256 RGBA PNG (6.6 KB), transparent elsewhere.

check.describe: Dark: a starry night-sky screen with 'Earth, right now' and 'Sun overhead at 15.3° S, 34.1° W' (at 14:00 UTC on 2 Nov 2026) at the top; a globe with a faint blue halo, lit from the left: Africa and Europe in daylight, the terminator running through Arabia and the Indian Ocean, Asia on the night side where Mumbai, Beijing and the other cities glow gold; labels London, Mumbai, Cape Town next to their dots. Later in time the globe has turned east (the view drifts west). A drag turns it. In June at 06:00 UTC the north pole is in daylight; in December at 22:00 UTC the south pole is. Light: the same globe on a pale blue-grey page (no stars, the blue halo kept as an atmosphere), dark ink text; the night half of the globe stays dark, the labels are white with a dark halo so they read on the globe and on the page. Mono: a hidden-line graticule sphere with the coastlines as line art, the city dots and labels, and the terminator as a solid great circle; no shading, no motion.
